Issued at 132 PM CST Tue Nov 24 2026

THIS AFTERNOON THROUGH WEDNESDAY MORNING...Early afternoon 
temperatures have recovered nicely following the cold start that 
featured a morning low of just 9 degrees at St. Cloud! Filtered
sunshine and light southerly flow have warmed midday 
temperatures into the low 30s across much of the area, with 
highs on track to climb a few degrees above freezing.

Our main weather concern over the next 24-hours is a potent 
shortwave currently digging southeast from Alberta into the Dakotas. 
The shortwave is progged to translate southeast towards Sioux Falls 
overnight. Mid-level warm air/moisture advection is increasing ahead 
of the incoming shortwave, which is evidenced by an uptick in radar 
echoes across western MN. No precipitation is reaching the surface 
yet, but that will change by late afternoon/early evening as a broad 
precipitation shield fills in from the northwest and top-down 
saturation occurs. Strong 1030s mb high pressure exists east of the 
anticipated snow shield, which will keep the eastern half of our MN 
counties (including the TC Metro) and western WI snowflake free 
tonight. However, confidence has increased in the first accumulating 
snow event of the season across southwestern MN. The overall picture 
has not changed much since the previous discussion, as the greatest 
potential for 1"+ of snow will be along and southwest of the MN 
River (highest amounts likely extend into WFO Sioux Falls area). 
Forecast soundings at CNB and RWF highlight a multi-hour period of 
moderate omega forcing located near/just below a shallow, but 
saturated DGZ around ~700 mb. This should generally be supportive
of snowfall rates approaching 0.25"/hr during the most intense 
period. CAM consensus from the REFS places the main snowfall 
axis southwest of our CWA border with WFO Sioux Falls. However, 
CAMs have a tendency to struggle capturing the overall extent of
the precipitation shield in WAA scenarios like this, so have 
leaned on the side of the deterministic/machine learning globals
to advertise a larger swath of light snow accumulation. As a 
result, we are rolling with a forecast that features QPF on the 
order of 0.02-0.08" along and west of a line from western 
Douglas county to western Faribault county, which yields 
snowfall amounts from a dusting to 1" (the highest amounts 
west of the MN River). In addition, we have boosted PoPs above 
the NBM and have also extended each respective PoP threshold 
east to allow for the larger region of light snow that our 
conceptual model favors.

Given an extended period of sub-freezing antecedent conditions, it 
is likely that snow will accumulate on untreated surfaces, which may 
result in slick travel tonight into Wednesday morning. Light snow 
will end by daybreak and temperatures are forecast to warm back to 
near freezing by 10 AM or so. 

WEDNESDAY AFTERNOON THROUGH EARLY NEXT WEEK...The shortwave 
responsible for the incoming round of light snow will continue to 
dig to the south across the eastern Plains, before pivoting and 
phasing with a southern stream wave to produce the headline making 
winter storm system across the Midwest/Ohio Valley. Impacts from 
this storm system are forecast to remain southeast of the forecast 
area, which is good news for local Thanksgiving travel. However, 
those traveling southeast into eastern IA/MO and IL should keep
an eye on the forecast as travel impacts are likely due to 
wintry weather. Quiet weather is anticipated for most of the 
second half of the week and the eastward translation of a strong
Pacific jet will yield a warming trend into the mid 40s for 
highs by Friday and Saturday. A weak frontal system is progged 
to advance across the Upper Midwest Friday night into Saturday 
and there are several ensemble members that feature light 
precipitation across eastern MN/western WI as this occurs. Would
largely favor liquid as the p-type given the anticipated 
temperature profile, however cooling at night could allow for a 
light wintry mix. Even so, this signal is currently muted and 
doesn't appear to be of much impact. NBM's ~20 PoPs are 
reasonable at this distance.

Our portion of the Upper Midwest will be between storm tracks 
over the weekend, which should support dry weather. Evolution of
the upper-air pattern beyond Sunday is uncertain, as solutions 
diverge regarding a mid-latitude system and associated 
warm/cold advection into the region. However, temperatures are 
likely to remain above normal into the start of December, which 
is depicted by NBM's highs in the 40s early next week and CPC's 
above normal 6-10 day temperature probabilities.
